questions.stem: Obedience differs from conformity because obedience involves:
options: copying a behaviour after watching a model be rewarded
responding to a direct order, usually from an authority figure
yielding to the unspoken pressure of a group of friends or peers
changing a private belief after hearing a persuasive message
questions.explanation: Obedience is following a direct instruction, usually from someone with authority. Conformity is yielding to group pressure, where no one necessarily gives an order.

questions.stem: Which three factors does research show influence obedience?
options: proximity, prestige of the authority figure and deindividuation
contiguity, contingency and reinforcement of the authority figure
attention, retention and reproduction of the authority figure
source, message and audience of the authority figure
questions.explanation: Obedience increases when the authority figure is close and prestigious and when the person feels anonymous or deindividuated, and decreases when the victim is close. The other sets of terms belong to learning and persuasion.

questions.stem: In Milgram's original study, 65% of participants gave what they believed was the maximum 450-volt shock. When the experimenter gave orders by telephone from another room, obedience dropped sharply. Which factor does this show?
options: the proximity of the learner to the teacher
the prestige of the location of the study
the deindividuation of the participant
the proximity of the authority figure
questions.explanation: When the authority figure was physically distant, it was easier to disobey, and full obedience fell to about 20%. The learner's position did not change in this variation.

questions.stem: When Milgram moved his study from Yale University to a run-down office building in a nearby city, full obedience fell from 65% to 47.5%. Which factor does this most clearly show?
options: the proximity of the authority figure
the proximity of the victim to the teacher
the deindividuation of the victim
the prestige of the authority figure
questions.explanation: A prestigious setting such as a well-known university adds legitimacy to the authority figure's orders. Removing that prestige reduced obedience, though nearly half still obeyed fully.

questions.stem: Obedience to destructive orders is more likely when people wear identical uniforms and are not known by name. Which concept explains this?
options: informational influence, a belief that others have more accurate knowledge
the norm of reciprocity, a felt obligation to repay a favour
deindividuation, a loss of the sense of personal identity and responsibility
internalisation, a lasting private acceptance of the group's beliefs and values
questions.explanation: Anonymity reduces self-awareness and the sense of personal responsibility, so people are more willing to follow orders they would otherwise refuse. Informational influence relates to conformity when a situation is ambiguous.

questions.stem: In one variation, Milgram's participants had to force the learner's hand onto a shock plate, and full obedience fell to 30%. Which statement best explains this result?
options: The participants were more deindividuated than in the original study
Seeing and touching the victim made the harm harder to deny or avoid
The authority figure was further away than in the original study
The setting had less prestige than the university laboratory
questions.explanation: Closeness to the victim makes their suffering vivid and personal, which makes obeying harder. The experimenter was still present and the setting unchanged, so the drop is explained by victim proximity.

questions.stem: What makes an investigation experimental rather than observational?
options: The researcher records behaviour as it occurs naturally without intervening
The researcher asks participants to describe their experiences in groups
The researcher collects data only from participants' written self-reports
The researcher manipulates an independent variable and measures its effect
questions.explanation: In an experiment the researcher deliberately changes the independent variable and measures the effect on the dependent variable, while controlling other variables. Observational designs record behaviour without manipulating anything.

questions.stem: Why are both Milgram's obedience studies and Zimbardo's prison study classed as experiments?
options: Each researcher set up and controlled the conditions participants experienced
Each researcher observed people in their everyday workplaces
Each study collected only qualitative data from focus groups
Each study used the Delphi technique to reach expert agreement
questions.explanation: Milgram manipulated features such as the proximity of the learner and the experimenter, and Zimbardo randomly assigned participants to be guards or prisoners. Both created controlled situations rather than observing natural behaviour.

questions.stem: In Milgram's variations, what was the dependent variable?
options: the level of obedience, measured by the maximum shock given
the physical proximity of the experimenter to the participant
the location in which the experiment was carried out
the instructions given by the experimenter to continue
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured: the highest voltage the participant went to before refusing. Proximity and location were independent variables that Milgram changed between variations.

questions.stem: What is a main advantage of the experimental design?
options: It allows cause-and-effect conclusions about variables
It always reflects how people behave in their everyday lives
It avoids every ethical problem in social research
It removes the need for a sample of participants
questions.explanation: Because the independent variable is manipulated while other variables are controlled, a change in the dependent variable can be attributed to it. Experiments often take place in artificial settings, so they do not always reflect everyday behaviour.

questions.stem: A critic says Milgram's laboratory setting was so artificial that the results may not reflect obedience in real life. This criticism concerns:
options: reliability
the independent variable
external validity
internal validity
questions.explanation: External validity is how well results generalise to people and settings beyond the study. Internal validity is whether the study really measured the effect of the independent variable.

questions.stem: Before beginning, Milgram's participants were told the study was about the effect of punishment on learning. This is an example of:
options: deception
debriefing
voluntary participation
confidentiality
questions.explanation: Participants were misled about the true purpose, which was to study obedience. Deception may hide the aim so that behaviour is natural, but it is one reason the study was criticised.

questions.stem: When participants in Milgram's study tried to stop, the experimenter used prods such as telling them they must go on. Which ethical right did this most clearly undermine?
options: the right to have personal information kept private
the right to be informed of the results of the research
the right to have data used only for the stated purpose
the right to withdraw at any time without explanation
questions.explanation: Participants should be able to leave a study at any time without pressure. The prods made withdrawing feel difficult. Privacy and access to results are separate rights that the prods did not affect.

questions.stem: Zimbardo's 1971 prison study was planned to run for two weeks. Why was it stopped after six days?
options: The prisoners organised a successful escape from the basement prison
The university ran out of funds to pay the participants
Guards were mistreating prisoners and some prisoners showed severe distress
The guards refused to enforce any of the prison rules they had been given
questions.explanation: Guards became increasingly abusive and several prisoners suffered acute emotional distress, so the study was ended early. Zimbardo later acknowledged that his role as prison superintendent compromised his responsibility for participants' welfare.

questions.stem: Which ethical criticism applies to Zimbardo's prison study in particular, rather than to Milgram's obedience study?
options: Participants were deceived about the true aim and believed they were harming someone
Participants were not fully debriefed about the electric shocks they thought they gave
The participants were all volunteers who answered an advertisement for paid research
The lead researcher also played a role in the situation, so he failed to protect participants
questions.explanation: Zimbardo acted as superintendent of the mock prison, which drew him into the situation and weakened his oversight of participants' wellbeing. Belief in harming someone with shocks applies to Milgram's study. Recruiting paid volunteers is not itself an ethical breach.

questions.stem: In Zimbardo's study, guards were randomly assigned to their role yet came to see the prisoners as less deserving of respect. What does this suggest about attitudes and behaviour?
options: Guards' attitudes stayed the same while only their behaviour changed
Acting out a role can change a person's attitudes to fit their behaviour
Attitudes always come first and then fully determine how a person behaves
Random assignment ensured guards already held negative attitudes
questions.explanation: The guards began with no particular attitude towards the prisoners, since roles were random. As they behaved harshly in their role, their attitudes shifted to match, showing behaviour can influence attitude.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes why Milgram's study has been defended despite the ethical criticisms?
options: No participant showed any signs of stress or tension during the study
The study was done in a natural setting, so no consent was needed
Participants were debriefed and it revealed important insights into obedience
Participants were told the true aim of the study before they agreed to take part
questions.explanation: Participants were debriefed and met the unharmed learner, and the findings changed understanding of how ordinary people can obey harmful orders. However, many participants showed visible stress, which is central to the criticisms.

questions.stem: Conformity is best defined as:
options: yielding to real or imagined group pressure
following a direct order from an authority figure
changing an attitude after reading a persuasive argument
learning a behaviour by watching a role model
questions.explanation: Conformity is changing behaviour or beliefs to match a group, even without any direct request. Following an authority's order is obedience.

questions.stem: A new employee laughs at her manager's jokes because everyone else does and she wants to be accepted, even though she finds them unfunny. This is an example of:
options: normative social influence
informational social influence
internalisation
obedience
questions.explanation: Normative social influence is conforming in order to be liked or accepted and to avoid rejection. Informational influence would involve believing the group has better knowledge about what is correct.

questions.stem: At a formal dinner, a guest unsure which fork to use watches the other guests and copies them. This is an example of:
options: compliance with an order
deindividuation
informational social influence
normative social influence
questions.explanation: When a situation is ambiguous, people look to others as a source of information about the correct behaviour. The guest copies to be correct, not mainly to be liked.

questions.stem: In Asch's line-judgement studies, participants conformed on about a third of critical trials. When they could write their answers privately, conformity fell sharply. What does this suggest?
options: Writing answers increased the prestige of the confederates in the group
Much of the conformity was due to normative influence, not changed perception
Most participants truly saw the lines as the group described them
Informational influence was strongest when answers were given in writing
questions.explanation: If participants had really seen the lines differently, they would have given the same wrong answers in private. The drop shows many conformed publicly to avoid standing out, which is normative influence.

questions.stem: In Asch's studies, conformity fell dramatically when one confederate gave the correct answer. Which factor affecting conformity does this show?
options: the deindividuation of the group
the loss of unanimity in the group
the larger size of the group
the higher status of the participant
questions.explanation: A single ally breaks the group's unanimity and makes it much easier to resist. The group size was unchanged in this variation.

questions.stem: Which individual characteristic is generally associated with greater conformity?
options: low self-esteem and a high need for social approval
high self-esteem and confidence in one's own judgement
expert knowledge of the task the group is judging
strong belief that one's own view is correct
questions.explanation: People who doubt themselves or strongly want approval are more likely to yield to group pressure. Confidence and expertise reduce reliance on the group's judgement.

questions.stem: Research comparing cultures suggests conformity tends to be higher in collectivist cultures than in individualist cultures. Which explanation fits this finding?
options: Collectivist cultures value group harmony, so agreeing with the group is seen positively
Collectivist cultures value independence, so disagreeing with the group is seen positively
Individualist cultures have larger groups, so there is more pressure to agree
Individualist cultures value obedience, so people follow orders more
questions.explanation: Where the group's goals and harmony are valued over personal ones, going along with others can be seen as a sign of respect rather than weakness. Individualist cultures place more value on standing out and independence.

questions.stem: A student publicly agrees with friends that a film was great, but privately still thinks it was boring. This is:
options: identification
informational influence
compliance
internalisation
questions.explanation: Compliance is a change in public behaviour without a change in private belief. Internalisation would mean the student genuinely came to like the film.

questions.stem: After joining a sports club, a young person adopts the club's dress and values while a member, because they admire the group, but drops them after leaving. This is:
options: obedience
identification
compliance
internalisation
questions.explanation: Identification is conforming to the behaviour and values of a group or role a person values, while they belong to it. It goes deeper than compliance but, unlike internalisation, does not last once the person leaves the group.

questions.stem: Which type of conformity is most likely to persist when the group is no longer present?
options: normative influence, because the person wants to be liked by the group
internalisation, because the person has privately accepted the group's view
compliance, because the person has publicly and repeatedly agreed with the group's view
identification, because the person admires the group while belonging to it
questions.explanation: In internalisation the group's view becomes part of the person's own beliefs, so it lasts without the group. Compliance is public only and fades once pressure is removed.

questions.stem: In an observational design, the investigator:
options: manipulates an independent variable and measures the result
randomly assigns participants to experimental and control groups
asks experts to rate items repeatedly until they agree
collects data by observing behaviour without manipulating variables
questions.explanation: Observational designs record behaviour, often in natural settings, without the researcher changing anything. Manipulating variables and random allocation are features of experiments.

questions.stem: A researcher records how often shoppers follow a sign telling them to queue, without interacting with them. What is the main advantage of this observational design?
options: Participants give informed consent before every observation is made
Behaviour is recorded in a natural setting, so ecological validity is high
The researcher can conclude that the sign caused the queuing behaviour
All extraneous variables are controlled by the researcher during the study
questions.explanation: Observing real behaviour where it naturally happens gives results that reflect everyday life. Because nothing is manipulated or controlled, cause-and-effect conclusions cannot be drawn.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of observational designs?
options: They can only be carried out inside a laboratory
They require the researcher to deceive every participant
They produce results with no relevance to real life
They cannot establish cause and effect between variables
questions.explanation: Without manipulation and control, many variables could explain an observed pattern, so causes cannot be identified. Observer bias and participants changing behaviour when watched are further problems.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to know whether wearing a uniform causes people to obey an instruction to pick up litter. Which design is most appropriate?
options: an experiment in which the instructor wears a uniform for half the participants
an observation of how often people pick up litter in a park on weekends
a focus group discussing how people feel about uniforms and authority
a survey asking people whether they usually obey people in uniform
questions.explanation: A causal question requires manipulating the independent variable, uniform or no uniform, while keeping other conditions the same. Observations and surveys could show a relationship but not a cause.

questions.stem: Ethnocentric bias in research occurs when an investigator:
options: uses a large, representative sample drawn from many cultures
judges another culture's behaviour by the standards of their own culture
records behaviour accurately using the norms of the culture being studied
asks the community being studied to help design the research questions
questions.explanation: Ethnocentrism treats one's own cultural norms as the standard, so behaviour that differs may be misinterpreted as deficient or abnormal. Involving the community helps to reduce this bias.

questions.stem: Early observational research on Aboriginal communities was often carried out by outsiders who interpreted behaviour through their own cultural norms. What is one likely effect of this?
options: Misleading, deficit-based conclusions that reinforced stereotypes
Highly accurate conclusions because the researchers were neutral outsiders
Increased trust in researchers among the communities that were studied
Greater control of the research by community members and Elders
questions.explanation: Interpreting behaviour through another culture's norms can lead to conclusions that portray a community as lacking or abnormal. Such research contributed to stereotypes and harmful policies, and to mistrust of researchers.

questions.stem: Which practice best reduces ethnocentric bias in research with Aboriginal communities?
options: Researchers keep their aims and methods hidden so that behaviour stays natural
Researchers rely on standard tests developed with non-Aboriginal samples
Researchers spend less time in the community to avoid influencing it
Communities take part in designing, conducting and interpreting the research
questions.explanation: Research led or co-designed by Aboriginal people respects self-determination and ensures behaviour is interpreted within its cultural context. Tests normed on other populations can carry the very bias the research needs to avoid.

questions.stem: Which ethical concern is especially important when research has been done on, rather than with, Aboriginal communities?
options: Communities may have received too many copies of the final report
Researchers may have spent too long consulting with community Elders
Researchers may have used too many participants from the community
Communities may not have given informed consent or benefited from the findings
questions.explanation: Historically, research was often done without meaningful consent, without sharing results, and without benefit to the community, and sometimes to its harm. Current guidelines emphasise consent, respect and community benefit.

questions.stem: Findings on obedience and conformity have been used to help understand how ordinary people took part in policies such as the forced removal of Aboriginal children. Which idea from obedience research is most relevant?
options: People resist authority most when an order comes from a government
People obey only when they are physically forced to by the authority
People may follow orders from legitimate authorities even when they cause harm
People obey only when they personally agree with the order they are being given
questions.explanation: Milgram found that many people will follow orders that harm others when the instruction comes from a legitimate authority. Government policy carried that kind of authority, which helps explain participation without excusing it.
